definition: To make someone used to something unpleasant through long exposure, so it bothers them less.
example: Years of rejection letters had inured the poet to disappointment.
nuance: Unlike accustom, inure is used for unpleasant things and suggests that repeated exposure has dulled a person's reaction.
prompt: A new resident has just moved into an apartment beside a busy airport.
options: Months of living there will inure him to the roar of jets overhead.
Standing too close to the runway could inure his eardrums for good.
He called an agent to inure his windows against noise damage.
Months there will inure him, so every plane startles him more than the last.
reasons: Repeated exposure over time dulls his reaction to an unpleasant noise, which fits the verb.
This confuses the verb with injure; it means hardening to hardship, not physical harm.
This mixes it up with insure; buying coverage has nothing to do with getting used to hardship.
Growing more startled is the reverse of becoming hardened to the noise.

practice.prompt: An apprentice starts working long shifts beside a bakery's hot ovens.
options: Summers beside the ovens slowly helped inure the apprentice to the heat.
She could barely inure the heat, so she left the kitchen after an hour.
One brief visit to the kitchen was enough to inure him to the heat for life.
Weeks at the ovens seemed to inure him, since the heat bothered him more each day.
reasons: Gradual, repeated exposure to discomfort that leaves her less bothered is exactly the idea.
This treats it like endure; the verb needs a person as its object, as in 'inure oneself to' something.
A single short visit cannot do it; the word implies long or repeated exposure.
Finding the heat harder to bear each day is the opposite of being hardened to it.
